arguments.issue: What is the correct date for adding a patent to the Patent Register under the Regulations?
arguments.claim: The date of submission, not eligibility confirmation, should be the date of addition to the Patent Register.
arguments.quote: Bayer notes that the Regulations do not contemplate any passage of time between the filing of a submission for an addition to the Patent Register and the actual addition to the Patent Register, and therefore the addition should be considered to have occurred on the day of the submission, regardless of when eligibility was confirmed.
arguments.weak_spot: The other side will argue the Regulations require eligibility confirmation before addition, as supported by Eli Lilly.

arguments.issue: Does Bayer’s interpretation of the Regulations prejudice Amgen?
arguments.claim: Amgen would not be prejudiced because it could amend its NDS to address newly listed patents.
arguments.quote: Bayer notes that Amgen would not have been prejudiced by its proposed interpretation of the Regulations because it would have been able to amend its NDS to address any patent that was confirmed to have been added to the Patent Register after it filed its NDS.
arguments.weak_spot: Amgen may argue that amending an NDS is burdensome or not always possible.

arguments.issue: Is the OSIP’s interpretation of the Regulations unbalanced or unreasonable?
arguments.claim: OSIP’s interpretation creates an imbalance between innovators and biosimilars, contrary to the Regulations’ purpose.
arguments.quote: Bayer argues that any other interpretation disturbs the balance between the interests of innovators and biosimilars that the Regulations strive to achieve.
arguments.weak_spot: The other side will argue the Regulations intentionally create this balance and that legislative intent supports the current interpretation.

arguments.issue: Should Eli Lilly be followed in this case?
arguments.claim: Eli Lilly is not binding, is distinguishable, and is unpersuasive in the present circumstances.
arguments.quote: Bayer argues that Eli Lilly is not binding on this Court, and that it is distinguishable and unpersuasive.

support.ref: Eli Lilly Canada Inc. v. Canada (Attorney General), 2009 FC 474
Paragraph 4(4)(f) and subsection 3(2.3) of the Regulations

arguments.weak_spot: The other side will argue Eli Lilly is directly on point and should be followed as persuasive authority.
